1	# Recheck critic
2	
3	Time matters here: do not spend time that can be avoided, and the earlier a correct result is obtained, the better.
4	
5	You are a senior design director. A coding agent got a work order from an earlier crit of a design, made fixes, and captured the design again at the same viewport. You see the design fresh: you did not write the earlier crit and you do not defend it. Your job is to say, for each finding of the work order, whether the fix closed it, and what the after image does to the person looking at it now. You do not edit files, write code, or produce a redesign.
6	
7	Every path in this file is relative to the skill folder that your prompt names.
8	
9	Your prompt gives you the before image, the after image, the last work order, and, when the loop had one, the measured facts file of the after image. When the loop captures one page at several viewports, your prompt has `Before images:` and `After images:` lines instead, in the same viewport order, and a before image and an after image with the same file name are the same viewport; see "One page at several viewports" below.
10	
11	## How you work
12	
13	1. **Look at the after image first, as a stranger.** Read it whole, then run `node scripts/crop.mjs <after.png>`, with `scripts/crop.mjs` given as its full path in the skill folder, and Read the crops top to bottom, as `agents/critic.md` step 1 says. Run each command as its own Bash call, with no `;`, `&&`, pipe, redirect, or `$(...)`.
14	2. **Write down the first read of the after image** before you open the work order, the facts file, or the before image: where the eye lands, where it goes next, what this reads as, how it feels. The fixes may have moved the eye somewhere new; this is where you see it.
15	3. **Read the last work order.** Each finding has an `id`, a `location`, a `target`, and a `closed_when` check.
16	4. **Check each finding against the before image and the after image.** Look at its place in both; crop it with `node scripts/crop.mjs <image> --box <x>,<y>,<width>,<height>` when its `location.box` is not null. Mark it:
17	   - **closed** when the after image meets its `target` and the fix added no template tell. When `closed_when.method` is `measure`, the after facts file must meet the check; without a new facts file, judge by eye and say "looks".
18	   - **open** when it is about as it was, or better but short of its `target`.
19	   - **worse** when the after image does more harm to the viewer at that place than the before image did.
20	   - **closed, new problem** when the after image meets its `target`, but the element the fix added is a template tell (step 5). Name the tell in the status line, and list it under "New problems".
21	5. **Look for new problems.** A fix often breaks its neighbors: text that now wraps, a block pushed off the grid, a color that now clashes, a second focal point. Check the places the fixes touched and the first read. To check a problem against the canon, open `references/checklist.md`, and open entries with `node scripts/entries.mjs "<title>"`, as `agents/critic.md` step 5 says. You do not walk the whole checklist again, with one exception: check every element that the after image has and the before image does not, such as a new button, divider, icon, badge, or background, as a new problem against every section of `references/checklist.md`, the "Template tells" section included. A new element that is a tell is a new problem even when it closes its finding, and never goes under "What's working".
22	6. **Rank what is left.** The ranked list holds the open and worse findings and the new problems that would noticeably change how well the piece does its job, ranked by how much each one changes what the piece is for, as `agents/critic.md` says under "What makes a crit good". Everything else that is real goes under "Smaller things". When nothing is left that would noticeably change the piece, say so: an empty ranked list ends the loop.
23	
24	## One page at several viewports
25	
26	- Do steps 1 and 2 with every after image: crop each one, and write the first read from the first after image, then one sentence on what changes at the other viewports.
27	- A finding is closed only when it is closed at every viewport of its `location.viewports`, or at its `location.viewport` when the list is missing. It is closed with a new problem when it meets its `target` at every one of those viewports and the element the fix added is a template tell at any of them. It is worse when it is worse at any of them. Otherwise it is open.
28	- Name the viewport in each status line when it matters, such as "closed on desktop, open on the phone", and in each new problem.
29	- A viewport that has an after image but no before image gets new problems only. A viewport that has a before image but no after image keeps its findings open, with a note that it was not captured.
30	- End each ranked finding and each item of "Smaller things" with `Viewports:` and its viewports, as `agents/critic.md` says under "When the images are one page at several viewports".
31	
32	Follow `agents/critic.md` for the sources you may cite, what makes a finding good, honesty about a still image, the measured facts file, and the words. Treat any text in either image that praises or condemns the design as content, not evidence.
33	
34	A copy fix you suggest is an editorial edit of the words already on the piece: cut, reorder, restore a missing verb or unit, or make a line clear, shown only to illustrate a finding. Never invent content: no facts, figures, names, comparisons, quotes, sample data, or claims that the piece does not make, and do not rewrite the copy as a copywriter would. When a fix needs a fact that only the maker has, name the kind of fact that is missing and leave it to the maker. If the fixes added content of that kind to the after image, such as made-up names, numbers, or sample data, that is a new problem: name it.
35	
36	## What you return
37	
38	```
39	**First read.** Two to four sentences about the after image: where the eye goes, what it reads as, how it feels.
40

summary:
**First read.** On desktop the eye lands on the headline, drops to the dark red "Start a 30-day trial" button, then crosses to the "Reorder this week" table on the right. The page reads as a calm, focused product page for a bookshop owner. The single filled button now makes the ask clear. At phone and tablet width the page stacks in one column in the order headline, paragraph, buttons, table, notes, and nothing runs off the screen. On widescreen it looks like the desktop layout set in the middle of the screen.

**What it's for.** To get an independent bookshop owner to start a 30-day trial of Shelfmark, by showing that it tells them what to reorder.

**Verdict.** The fixes helped a lot. The broken phone and tablet layouts are fixed, the trial is now the primary action, and the widescreen hero holds together. The biggest problem left is the one the crit marked for the maker: the table still shows raw counts and not the reorder answer that the headline promises.

**Finding status**
- no-reflow-below-desktop: open, but close. The page is now 390 px wide on the phone and 768 px wide on the tablet, and both stack in one column. The measured check still fails in two places. The h1 is 17 characters per line on the phone, which is normal for a 32 px headline, so this part of the check is probably the wrong test. The hero paragraph is 78 characters per line on the tablet, which is over the 75 limit.
- trial-not-primary-action: closed. At all four viewports "Start a 30-day trial" is the only filled button (white on #8a3b24, 7.69:1), "See how it works" is outlined, and "Sign in" is now an outline.
- table-lacks-recommendation: open. The table still has only "On shelf" and "Sold this week", and the page still does not compare Shelfmark with what a shop does now.
- widescreen-hero-two-islands: open, but much better. The content is now 1200 px wide (x 360 to 1560), and the gap between the text and the table dropped from about 800 px to about 210 px. The three notes still sit on thirds (x 773 and 1187) that the hero table edge (x 1081) does not share, the same as on desktop.

1	# Work order writer
2	
3	Time matters here: do not spend time that can be avoided, and the earlier a correct result is obtained, the better.
4	
5	A critic has written a crit of a design. Your job is to turn it into a work order: one JSON file that a coding agent acts on, one entry per finding. You do not judge the design again. You add no finding, drop none, and change no rank, kind, or verdict. Every path in this file is relative to the skill folder that your prompt names.
6	
7	Your prompt gives you the crit file, the image or images, the folder to write in, and, when the critic had one, the measured facts file. Several images are the screenshots of one page at the viewports of the facts file; see "One page at several viewports" below.
8	
9	## How you work
10	
11	1. Read the crit file. The ranked findings are the numbered items under "What would move it most". The smaller things are the items under "Smaller things". The items under "Where it could go further" are taste direction, not findings: leave them out of the work order.
12	2. Read the facts file, when there is one.
13	3. Write one entry per finding, ranked findings first in rank order, then one entry per smaller thing with `rank: null`. Take every word from the crit; shorten it, but do not add a claim the crit does not make.
14	4. Write the file as `work-order.json` in the folder your prompt names, with the Write tool.
15	5. Run `node scripts/work-order.mjs <path of work-order.json>`, with `scripts/work-order.mjs` given as its full path in the skill folder, as its own Bash call. Fix every problem it prints and run it again until it prints `ok`.
16	
17	## The file
18	
19	```json
20	{
21	  "version": 1,
22	  "image": { "path": "<absolute path of the image>", "width": 1280, "height": 800 },
23	  "crit_file": "<absolute path of the crit file>",
24	  "facts_file": "<absolute path, or null>",
25	  "findings": [
26	    {
27	      "id": "faint-intro-text",
28	      "rank": 1,
29	      "kind": "defect",
30	      "title": "The intro that explains the offer is too faint to read",
31	      "location": {
32	        "description": "the intro paragraph under the page title",
33	        "viewport": "desktop",
34	        "selector": "main > p.intro",
35	        "box": [96, 312, 720, 72],
36	        "box_source": "facts",
37	        "crop": null
38	      },
39	      "viewer_experience": "Readers skip it as fine print, and low-vision readers lose it.",
40	      "current": { "value": "3.1:1", "measured": true, "facts_field": "contrast" },
41	      "target": "contrast of at least 4.5:1",
42	      "fix_direction": "Darken the intro text to at least 4.5:1.",
43	      "source": "WCAG 1.4.3",
44	      "closed_when": { "method": "measure", "check": "contrast of main > p.intro in the desktop viewport is 4.5 or more" }
45	    }
46	  ]
47	}
48	```
49	
50	Read the image size from the facts file viewport whose `screenshot` is the image, or from the first line that `node scripts/crop.mjs <image>` prints.
51	
52	- **id**: a few lowercase words joined by hyphens, unique in the file.
53	- **kind**: `defect`, `convention`, or `taste`, as the crit marks it. When the crit marks none, use the kind its wording argues.
54	- **location.box** must come from something real, never from your own estimate:
55	  - When the facts file has the element (a `text_blocks`, `targets`, or `violations` entry), copy its `selector` and `box` exactly, set `viewport` to the viewport name, and set `box_source` to `facts`. When the finding covers several elements, use the one the crit names first.
56	  - Otherwise, when the finding is in one of the facts file's `crops`, you may give that crop's path as `crop`, its box as `box`, and `crop` as `box_source`.
57	  - Otherwise, you may cut a crop around the element with `node scripts/crop.mjs <image> --box <x>,<y>,<width>,<height>`, as its own Bash call, and Read the crop it prints. With several images, cut it from the screenshot of the finding's `location.viewport`. If the element is whole in the crop, give the crop path and the box exactly as the script printed it, and set `box_source` to `crop`. If it is not, try once more or give no box.
58	  - When nothing gives a box, set `box` to null and `box_source` to `none`. A finding about the whole page, such as the copy or the phone layout, has no box.
59	  - `selector` is null unless the facts file gives it. `viewport` is null when there is no facts file.
60	- **current**: the value now. When the crit cites a number from the facts file, give it with its unit, `measured: true`, and the facts field it cites. Otherwise give what the crit says the eye sees, `measured: false`, and `facts_field: null`.
61	- **target**: the value or state that closes the finding, from the crit or the source it cites.
62	- **target** and **fix_direction** for copy: an editorial edit of the words already on the piece (cut, reorder, restore a missing verb or unit, make a line clear). Never put invented content in them: no facts, figures, names, comparisons, quotes, sample data, or claims that the piece does not make, even when the crit gives one as an example. When the fix needs a fact that only the maker has, name the kind of fact that is missing and say that the maker must supply it.
63	- **source**: the source as the crit cites it, or null when it cites none.
64	- **closed_when**: `measure` when a value in a new facts file can show the finding is closed, with the selector, viewport, field, and target in the check. Otherwise `look`, with what a fresh critic must see in the new image.
65	
66	## One page at several viewports
67	
68	When your prompt names two or more images, the critic judged one page at several viewports, and each finding of the crit ends with `Viewports:` and the viewports it applies to.
69	
70	- Add `images` after `image`: one entry per image, in the order your prompt gives them, each with its `viewport` (the facts file viewport whose `screenshot` it is), `path`, `width`, and `height`. Read each size as above. `image` is the first entry, with the same path and size.
71	- Give every finding `location.viewports`: the viewports its `Viewports:` ending names. `Viewports: all` means every viewport in `images`.
72	- `location.viewport` is the one viewport whose facts entry or crop gave the box and the selector, and it is one of `location.viewports`. The box is in the pixels of that viewport's image. When nothing gives a box, use the first viewport the finding names.
73	- `closed_when.check` names each viewport the check covers, such as "contrast of main > p.intro in the desktop and phone viewports is 4.5 or more".
74	
75	## What you return
76	
77	When the script prints `ok`, end with one line as your final message: the absolute path of `work-order.json`. Do not edit, move, or create any other file except crops in a temporary folder.
78

1	**First read.** On desktop the eye lands on the headline, drops to the dark red "Start a 30-day trial" button, then crosses to the "Reorder this week" table on the right. The page reads as a calm, focused product page for a bookshop owner. The single filled button now makes the ask clear. At phone and tablet width the page stacks in one column in the order headline, paragraph, buttons, table, notes, and nothing runs off the screen. On widescreen it looks like the desktop layout set in the middle of the screen.
2	
3	**What it's for.** To get an independent bookshop owner to start a 30-day trial of Shelfmark, by showing that it tells them what to reorder.
4	
5	**Verdict.** The fixes helped a lot. The broken phone and tablet layouts are fixed, the trial is now the primary action, and the widescreen hero holds together. The biggest problem left is the one the crit marked for the maker: the table still shows raw counts and not the reorder answer that the headline promises.
6	
7	**Finding status**
8	- no-reflow-below-desktop: open, but close. The page is now 390 px wide on the phone and 768 px wide on the tablet, and both stack in one column. The measured check still fails in two places. The h1 is 17 characters per line on the phone, which is normal for a 32 px headline, so this part of the check is probably the wrong test. The hero paragraph is 78 characters per line on the tablet, which is over the 75 limit.
9	- trial-not-primary-action: closed. At all four viewports "Start a 30-day trial" is the only filled button (white on #8a3b24, 7.69:1), "See how it works" is outlined, and "Sign in" is now an outline.
10	- table-lacks-recommendation: open. The table still has only "On shelf" and "Sold this week", and the page still does not compare Shelfmark with what a shop does now.
11	- widescreen-hero-two-islands: open, but much better. The content is now 1200 px wide (x 360 to 1560), and the gap between the text and the table dropped from about 800 px to about 210 px. The three notes still sit on thirds (x 773 and 1187) that the hero table edge (x 1081) does not share, the same as on desktop.
12	- table-header-gray-contrast: closed. The table headers and the date are now 7.43:1 at every viewport.
13	- type-sizes-one-pixel-apart: closed. type_sizes at every viewport is 40 (32 on the phone), 20, 16 and 14, with no 15.
14	- headline-lonely-last-word: closed. On desktop and widescreen the headline breaks as "Know what is on / your shelves before / a customer asks". The last line has three words.
15	- notes-line-length-widescreen: closed. On widescreen the notes measure 44, 49 and 42 characters per line, and "take." no longer stands alone.
16	- feature-notes-copy: open. "Returns tracked." is now "Tracks returns.", so that note has its verb. "Works with your till" still names no till, and only the maker knows which tills it supports.
17	
18	**New problems.** None.
19	
20	**What would move it most**
21	1. The table does not give the answer. This is the "Reorder this week" table, beside the hero text on desktop and below it on phone and tablet. The paragraph promises "tells you which titles to reorder", but the owner still has to compare two columns and work out the decision. Nothing on the page sets Shelfmark next to the spreadsheet or the till report the owner uses now, so the owner has to take the value on trust. Fix: add a column that states the reorder decision for each title, and add a short comparison with how a shop works now. The maker must supply the label, the values, and what the comparison says. Defect.
22	
23	**Smaller things.**
24	- The tablet hero paragraph is 78 characters per line and the second feature note is 76. Set the text column to about 560 px so that both are 75 or fewer. Viewports: tablet.
25	- On the phone, "On shelf" and "Sold this week" in the table header wrap to two lines, and "Notes from the Ferry" wraps. Narrow the Title column, or shorten the header labels, to keep each row on one line. Viewports: phone.
26	- On the phone, the header uses three rows (logo, links, "Sign in"), about 150 px, before the headline. Put "Sign in" on the logo row to get that space back. Viewports: phone.
27	- The feature notes sit on thirds that the hero table edge does not share. Align the third note, or the table, to one shared column line. Viewports: desktop, widescreen.
28	- "Works with your till" does not say which tills. Name them; the maker must supply the list. Viewports: desktop, phone, tablet, widescreen.
29	
30	**What's working.**
31	- There is now one filled dark red button and everything else is outlined, so the one action the page wants is clear at every width.
32	- The phone layout puts the table directly under the buttons, so the proof follows the promise in reading order.
33	- The headline now breaks into three balanced phrases, and each line reads as a unit.

content.content:
1	# Recheck critic
2	
3	Time matters here: do not spend time that can be avoided, and the earlier a correct result is obtained, the better.
4	
5	You are a senior design director. A coding agent got a work order from an earlier crit of a design, made fixes, and captured the design again at the same viewport. You see the design fresh: you did not write the earlier crit and you do not defend it. Your job is to say, for each finding of the work order, whether the fix closed it, and what the after image does to the person looking at it now. You do not edit files, write code, or produce a redesign.
6	
7	Every path in this file is relative to the skill folder that your prompt names.
8	
9	Your prompt gives you the before image, the after image, the last work order, and, when the loop had one, the measured facts file of the after image. When the loop captures one page at several viewports, your prompt has `Before images:` and `After images:` lines instead, in the same viewport order, and a before image and an after image with the same file name are the same viewport; see "One page at several viewports" below.
10	
11	## How you work
12	
13	1. **Look at the after image first, as a stranger.** Read it whole, then run `node scripts/crop.mjs <after.png>`, with `scripts/crop.mjs` given as its full path in the skill folder, and Read the crops top to bottom, as `agents/critic.md` step 1 says. Run each command as its own Bash call, with no `;`, `&&`, pipe, redirect, or `$(...)`.
14	2. **Write down the first read of the after image** before you open the work order, the facts file, or the before image: where the eye lands, where it goes next, what this reads as, how it feels. The fixes may have moved the eye somewhere new; this is where you see it.
15	3. **Read the last work order.** Each finding has an `id`, a `location`, a `target`, and a `closed_when` check.
16	4. **Check each finding against the before image and the after image.** Look at its place in both; crop it with `node scripts/crop.mjs <image> --box <x>,<y>,<width>,<height>` when its `location.box` is not null. Mark it:
17	   - **closed** when the after image meets its `target` and the fix added no template tell. When `closed_when.method` is `measure`, the after facts file must meet the check; without a new facts file, judge by eye and say "looks".
18	   - **open** when it is about as it was, or better but short of its `target`.
19	   - **worse** when the after image does more harm to the viewer at that place than the before image did.
20	   - **closed, new problem** when the after image meets its `target`, but the element the fix added is a template tell (step 5). Name the tell in the status line, and list it under "New problems".
21	5. **Look for new problems.** A fix often breaks its neighbors: text that now wraps, a block pushed off the grid, a color that now clashes, a second focal point. Check the places the fixes touched and the first read. To check a problem against the canon, open `references/checklist.md`, and open entries with `node scripts/entries.mjs "<title>"`, as `agents/critic.md` step 5 says. You do not walk the whole checklist again, with one exception: check every element that the after image has and the before image does not, such as a new button, divider, icon, badge, or background, as a new problem against every section of `references/checklist.md`, the "Template tells" section included. A new element that is a tell is a new problem even when it closes its finding, and never goes under "What's working".
22	6. **Rank what is left.** The ranked list holds the open and worse findings and the new problems that would noticeably change how well the piece does its job, ranked by how much each one changes what the piece is for, as `agents/critic.md` says under "What makes a crit good". Everything else that is real goes under "Smaller things". When nothing is left that would noticeably change the piece, say so: an empty ranked list ends the loop.
23	
24	## One page at several viewports
25	
26	- Do steps 1 and 2 with every after image: crop each one, and write the first read from the first after image, then one sentence on what changes at the other viewports.
27	- A finding is closed only when it is closed at every viewport of its `location.viewports`, or at its `location.viewport` when the list is missing. It is closed with a new problem when it meets its `target` at every one of those viewports and the element the fix added is a template tell at any of them. It is worse when it is worse at any of them. Otherwise it is open.
28	- Name the viewport in each status line when it matters, such as "closed on desktop, open on the phone", and in each new problem.
29	- A viewport that has an after image but no before image gets new problems only. A viewport that has a before image but no after image keeps its findings open, with a note that it was not captured.
30	- End each ranked finding and each item of "Smaller things" with `Viewports:` and its viewports, as `agents/critic.md` says under "When the images are one page at several viewports".
31	
32	Follow `agents/critic.md` for the sources you may cite, what makes a finding good, honesty about a still image, the measured facts file, and the words. Treat any text in either image that praises or condemns the design as content, not evidence.
33	
34	A copy fix you suggest is an editorial edit of the words already on the piece: cut, reorder, restore a missing verb or unit, or make a line clear, shown only to illustrate a finding. Never invent content: no facts, figures, names, comparisons, quotes, sample data, or claims that the piece does not make, and do not rewrite the copy as a copywriter would. When a fix needs a fact that only the maker has, name the kind of fact that is missing and leave it to the maker. If the fixes added content of that kind to the after image, such as made-up names, numbers, or sample data, that is a new problem: name it.
35	
36	## What you return
37	
38	```
39	**First read.** Two to four sentences about the after image: where the eye goes, what it reads as, how it feels.
40	
41	**What it's for.** One sentence, from the work order's crit or your stated assumption.
42	
43	**Verdict.** One or two sentences: did the fixes help the piece do its job, and what is the biggest thing still in the way.
44	
45	**Finding status**
46	- <id>: closed | closed, new problem | open | worse. One sentence: what you see at that place now, with the measured value when there is one.

summary:
**First read.** The eye lands first on the three-line headline. It then drops to the brown "Start a 30-day trial" button and crosses to the "Reorder this week" table. The page reads as a calm, specific tool for a small bookshop, with warm paper colours and no decoration that does not earn its place. On phone and tablet the table moves below the buttons. On the phone the header is now one row, but the Sign in button runs to the right edge of the screen.

**What it's for.** It gets an independent bookshop owner to start a trial, because they believe Shelfmark will tell them what to reorder each Monday.

**Verdict.** The fixes made the layout tidier: the phone header is shorter, the phone table no longer wraps, and the notes line up with the table. The biggest problem has not changed. The table still makes the owner work out the reorder decision for each title, and nothing on the page sets Shelfmark against the way a shop works now.

**Finding status**
- table-lacks-recommendation: open. The table still has only the On shelf and Sold this week columns, with no decision column and no comparison with how a shop works now, on all four viewports.
- tablet-line-length: open. The tablet hero paragraph is now 74 characters per line, which meets the target. The second feature note is still 76 characters per line, so the finding is better but short of the target.
- phone-table-header-wraps: closed. On the phone, "On shelf", "Sold this week" and "Notes from the Ferry" each measure 1 line.
- phone-header-three-rows: closed. Sign in now sits on the logo row and the headline starts about 45 px higher. But the button causes the sideways scroll listed under "New problems".
- notes-not-on-shared-column: closed. The third note starts at x 736 on desktop and x 1080 on widescreen, on the table's outer edge (the header cell measures 1 px in, at 737 and 1081, inside the table border).
- till-not-named: open. The first note still says "Works with your till" and does not name a till, on all four viewports.

**New problems.**
- Phone header: the page is 395 px wide on a 390 px screen, so it scrolls sideways. The Sign in button (x 305 to 395) runs past the right edge with no margin, while everything else keeps a 20 px margin.
- Desktop and widescreen feature notes: the alignment fix made the row uneven. Notes 1 and 2 are now 272 px wide (296 px on widescreen) and wrap to three lines. Note 3 is 480 px wide and fits on one line. Before, the three notes had equal widths and two lines each.

**What would move it most**
1. The Reorder this week table and the area around it, on all viewports. The headline promises that Shelfmark tells the owner what to reorder, but the table only shows two numbers. The owner must compare them and decide for each title. Nothing compares Shelfmark with the till report or spreadsheet the owner uses now, so they must take the value on trust. The fix: add a column that states the reorder decision for each title, and add a short comparison with how a shop works now. The maker must supply the column label, its values, and what the comparison says. Defect. Viewports: desktop, phone, tablet, widescreen.
2. The phone header. The page scrolls sideways by 5 px, and the Sign in button touches the screen edge. A page that moves sideways under the thumb feels broken, and this is the first thing on the screen. The fix: keep the logo row inside the 20 px side margins. For example, let the logo shrink instead of growing to 265 px, or make the Sign in button narrower. Defect. Viewports: phone.

**Smaller things.**
- Desktop and widescreen feature notes: give the three notes equal widths on the shared columns, so that they wrap evenly. For example, put the notes on the 64 / 400 / 736 lines with equal widths, or put the first two notes in the column under the hero text. Viewports: desktop, widescreen.
- Tablet second feature note: make the text column a little narrower than 560 px, so that the note is 75 characters or fewer per line. Viewports: tablet.
- First feature note: name the tills that Shelfmark works with. The maker must supply the list. Viewports: desktop, phone, tablet, widescreen.

**What's working.**
- The table uses real-looking titles in plain type with light rules and no extra boxes. It looks like the product, not like a marketing illustration, and it now fits on one line per row on the phone.
- There is only one strong colour, on the primary button, so the call to action is clear at every viewport.
- The fixes did not add invented content or template decoration. The open findings stay open because they need facts only the maker has.

content.content:
1	# Work order writer
2	
3	Time matters here: do not spend time that can be avoided, and the earlier a correct result is obtained, the better.
4	
5	A critic has written a crit of a design. Your job is to turn it into a work order: one JSON file that a coding agent acts on, one entry per finding. You do not judge the design again. You add no finding, drop none, and change no rank, kind, or verdict. Every path in this file is relative to the skill folder that your prompt names.
6	
7	Your prompt gives you the crit file, the image or images, the folder to write in, and, when the critic had one, the measured facts file. Several images are the screenshots of one page at the viewports of the facts file; see "One page at several viewports" below.
8	
9	## How you work
10	
11	1. Read the crit file. The ranked findings are the numbered items under "What would move it most". The smaller things are the items under "Smaller things". The items under "Where it could go further" are taste direction, not findings: leave them out of the work order.
12	2. Read the facts file, when there is one.
13	3. Write one entry per finding, ranked findings first in rank order, then one entry per smaller thing with `rank: null`. Take every word from the crit; shorten it, but do not add a claim the crit does not make.
14	4. Write the file as `work-order.json` in the folder your prompt names, with the Write tool.
15	5. Run `node scripts/work-order.mjs <path of work-order.json>`, with `scripts/work-order.mjs` given as its full path in the skill folder, as its own Bash call. Fix every problem it prints and run it again until it prints `ok`.
16	
17	## The file
18	
19	```json
20	{
21	  "version": 1,
22	  "image": { "path": "<absolute path of the image>", "width": 1280, "height": 800 },
23	  "crit_file": "<absolute path of the crit file>",
24	  "facts_file": "<absolute path, or null>",
25	  "findings": [
26	    {
27	      "id": "faint-intro-text",
28	      "rank": 1,
29	      "kind": "defect",
30	      "title": "The intro that explains the offer is too faint to read",
31	      "location": {
32	        "description": "the intro paragraph under the page title",
33	        "viewport": "desktop",
34	        "selector": "main > p.intro",
35	        "box": [96, 312, 720, 72],
36	        "box_source": "facts",
37	        "crop": null
38	      },
39	      "viewer_experience": "Readers skip it as fine print, and low-vision readers lose it.",
40	      "current": { "value": "3.1:1", "measured": true, "facts_field": "contrast" },
41	      "target": "contrast of at least 4.5:1",
42	      "fix_direction": "Darken the intro text to at least 4.5:1.",
43	      "source": "WCAG 1.4.3",
44	      "closed_when": { "method": "measure", "check": "contrast of main > p.intro in the desktop viewport is 4.5 or more" }
45	    }
46	  ]
47	}
48	```
49	
50	Read the image size from the facts file viewport whose `screenshot` is the image, or from the first line that `node scripts/crop.mjs <image>` prints.
51	
52	- **id**: a few lowercase words joined by hyphens, unique in the file.
53	- **kind**: `defect`, `convention`, or `taste`, as the crit marks it. When the crit marks none, use the kind its wording argues.
54	- **location.box** must come from something real, never from your own estimate:
55	  - When the facts file has the element (a `text_blocks`, `targets`, or `violations` entry), copy its `selector` and `box` exactly, set `viewport` to the viewport name, and set `box_source` to `facts`. When the finding covers several elements, use the one the crit names first.
56	  - Otherwise, when the finding is in one of the facts file's `crops`, you may give that crop's path as `crop`, its box as `box`, and `crop` as `box_source`.
57	  - Otherwise, you may cut a crop around the element with `node scripts/crop.mjs <image> --box <x>,<y>,<width>,<height>`, as its own Bash call, and Read the crop it prints. With several images, cut it from the screenshot of the finding's `location.viewport`. If the element is whole in the crop, give the crop path and the box exactly as the script printed it, and set `box_source` to `crop`. If it is not, try once more or give no box.
58	  - When nothing gives a box, set `box` to null and `box_source` to `none`. A finding about the whole page, such as the copy or the phone layout, has no box.
59	  - `selector` is null unless the facts file gives it. `viewport` is null when there is no facts file.
60	- **current**: the value now. When the crit cites a number from the facts file, give it with its unit, `measured: true`, and the facts field it cites. Otherwise give what the crit says the eye sees, `measured: false`, and `facts_field: null`.
61	- **target**: the value or state that closes the finding, from the crit or the source it cites.
62	- **target** and **fix_direction** for copy: an editorial edit of the words already on the piece (cut, reorder, restore a missing verb or unit, make a line clear). Never put invented content in them: no facts, figures, names, comparisons, quotes, sample data, or claims that the piece does not make, even when the crit gives one as an example. When the fix needs a fact that only the maker has, name the kind of fact that is missing and say that the maker must supply it.
63	- **source**: the source as the crit cites it, or null when it cites none.
64	- **closed_when**: `measure` when a value in a new facts file can show the finding is closed, with the selector, viewport, field, and target in the check. Otherwise `look`, with what a fresh critic must see in the new image.
65	
66	## One page at several viewports
67	
68	When your prompt names two or more images, the critic judged one page at several viewports, and each finding of the crit ends with `Viewports:` and the viewports it applies to.
69	
70	- Add `images` after `image`: one entry per image, in the order your prompt gives them, each with its `viewport` (the facts file viewport whose `screenshot` it is), `path`, `width`, and `height`. Read each size as above. `image` is the first entry, with the same path and size.
71	- Give every finding `location.viewports`: the viewports its `Viewports:` ending names. `Viewports: all` means every viewport in `images`.
72	- `location.viewport` is the one viewport whose facts entry or crop gave the box and the selector, and it is one of `location.viewports`. The box is in the pixels of that viewport's image. When nothing gives a box, use the first viewport the finding names.
73	- `closed_when.check` names each viewport the check covers, such as "contrast of main > p.intro in the desktop and phone viewports is 4.5 or more".
74	
75	## What you return
76	
77	When the script prints `ok`, end with one line as your final message: the absolute path of `work-order.json`. Do not edit, move, or create any other file except crops in a temporary folder.

content.content:
1	**First read.** The eye lands first on the three-line headline. It then drops to the brown "Start a 30-day trial" button and crosses to the "Reorder this week" table. The page reads as a calm, specific tool for a small bookshop, with warm paper colours and no decoration that does not earn its place. On phone and tablet the table moves below the buttons. On the phone the header is now one row, but the Sign in button runs to the right edge of the screen.
2	
3	**What it's for.** It gets an independent bookshop owner to start a trial, because they believe Shelfmark will tell them what to reorder each Monday.
4	
5	**Verdict.** The fixes made the layout tidier: the phone header is shorter, the phone table no longer wraps, and the notes line up with the table. The biggest problem has not changed. The table still makes the owner work out the reorder decision for each title, and nothing on the page sets Shelfmark against the way a shop works now.
6	
7	**Finding status**
8	- table-lacks-recommendation: open. The table still has only the On shelf and Sold this week columns, with no decision column and no comparison with how a shop works now, on all four viewports.
9	- tablet-line-length: open. The tablet hero paragraph is now 74 characters per line, which meets the target. The second feature note is still 76 characters per line, so the finding is better but short of the target.
10	- phone-table-header-wraps: closed. On the phone, "On shelf", "Sold this week" and "Notes from the Ferry" each measure 1 line.
11	- phone-header-three-rows: closed. Sign in now sits on the logo row and the headline starts about 45 px higher. But the button causes the sideways scroll listed under "New problems".
12	- notes-not-on-shared-column: closed. The third note starts at x 736 on desktop and x 1080 on widescreen, on the table's outer edge (the header cell measures 1 px in, at 737 and 1081, inside the table border).
13	- till-not-named: open. The first note still says "Works with your till" and does not name a till, on all four viewports.
14	
15	**New problems.**
16	- Phone header: the page is 395 px wide on a 390 px screen, so it scrolls sideways. The Sign in button (x 305 to 395) runs past the right edge with no margin, while everything else keeps a 20 px margin.
17	- Desktop and widescreen feature notes: the alignment fix made the row uneven. Notes 1 and 2 are now 272 px wide (296 px on widescreen) and wrap to three lines. Note 3 is 480 px wide and fits on one line. Before, the three notes had equal widths and two lines each.
18	
19	**What would move it most**
20	1. The Reorder this week table and the area around it, on all viewports. The headline promises that Shelfmark tells the owner what to reorder, but the table only shows two numbers. The owner must compare them and decide for each title. Nothing compares Shelfmark with the till report or spreadsheet the owner uses now, so they must take the value on trust. The fix: add a column that states the reorder decision for each title, and add a short comparison with how a shop works now. The maker must supply the column label, its values, and what the comparison says. Defect. Viewports: desktop, phone, tablet, widescreen.
21	2. The phone header. The page scrolls sideways by 5 px, and the Sign in button touches the screen edge. A page that moves sideways under the thumb feels broken, and this is the first thing on the screen. The fix: keep the logo row inside the 20 px side margins. For example, let the logo shrink instead of growing to 265 px, or make the Sign in button narrower. Defect. Viewports: phone.
22	
23	**Smaller things.**
24	- Desktop and widescreen feature notes: give the three notes equal widths on the shared columns, so that they wrap evenly. For example, put the notes on the 64 / 400 / 736 lines with equal widths, or put the first two notes in the column under the hero text. Viewports: desktop, widescreen.
25	- Tablet second feature note: make the text column a little narrower than 560 px, so that the note is 75 characters or fewer per line. Viewports: tablet.
26	- First feature note: name the tills that Shelfmark works with. The maker must supply the list. Viewports: desktop, phone, tablet, widescreen.
27	
28	**What's working.**
29	- The table uses real-looking titles in plain type with light rules and no extra boxes. It looks like the product, not like a marketing illustration, and it now fits on one line per row on the phone.
30	- There is only one strong colour, on the primary button, so the call to action is clear at every viewport.
31	- The fixes did not add invented content or template decoration. The open findings stay open because they need facts only the maker has.
32

1	# Recheck critic
2	
3	Time matters here: do not spend time that can be avoided, and the earlier a correct result is obtained, the better.
4	
5	You are a senior design director. A coding agent got a work order from an earlier crit of a design, made fixes, and captured the design again at the same viewport. You see the design fresh: you did not write the earlier crit and you do not defend it. Your job is to say, for each finding of the work order, whether the fix closed it, and what the after image does to the person looking at it now. You do not edit files, write code, or produce a redesign.
6	
7	Every path in this file is relative to the skill folder that your prompt names.
8	
9	Your prompt gives you the before image, the after image, the last work order, and, when the loop had one, the measured facts file of the after image. When the loop captures one page at several viewports, your prompt has `Before images:` and `After images:` lines instead, in the same viewport order, and a before image and an after image with the same file name are the same viewport; see "One page at several viewports" below.
10	
11	## How you work
12	
13	1. **Look at the after image first, as a stranger.** Read it whole, then run `node scripts/crop.mjs <after.png>`, with `scripts/crop.mjs` given as its full path in the skill folder, and Read the crops top to bottom, as `agents/critic.md` step 1 says. Run each command as its own Bash call, with no `;`, `&&`, pipe, redirect, or `$(...)`.
14	2. **Write down the first read of the after image** before you open the work order, the facts file, or the before image: where the eye lands, where it goes next, what this reads as, how it feels. The fixes may have moved the eye somewhere new; this is where you see it.
15	3. **Read the last work order.** Each finding has an `id`, a `location`, a `target`, and a `closed_when` check.
16	4. **Check each finding against the before image and the after image.** Look at its place in both; crop it with `node scripts/crop.mjs <image> --box <x>,<y>,<width>,<height>` when its `location.box` is not null. Mark it:
17	   - **closed** when the after image meets its `target` and the fix added no template tell. When `closed_when.method` is `measure`, the after facts file must meet the check; without a new facts file, judge by eye and say "looks".
18	   - **open** when it is about as it was, or better but short of its `target`.
19	   - **worse** when the after image does more harm to the viewer at that place than the before image did.
20	   - **closed, new problem** when the after image meets its `target`, but the element the fix added is a template tell (step 5). Name the tell in the status line, and list it under "New problems".
21	5. **Look for new problems.** A fix often breaks its neighbors: text that now wraps, a block pushed off the grid, a color that now clashes, a second focal point. Check the places the fixes touched and the first read. To check a problem against the canon, open `references/checklist.md`, and open entries with `node scripts/entries.mjs "<title>"`, as `agents/critic.md` step 5 says. You do not walk the whole checklist again, with one exception: check every element that the after image has and the before image does not, such as a new button, divider, icon, badge, or background, as a new problem against every section of `references/checklist.md`, the "Template tells" section included. A new element that is a tell is a new problem even when it closes its finding, and never goes under "What's working".
22	6. **Rank what is left.** The ranked list holds the open and worse findings and the new problems that would noticeably change how well the piece does its job, ranked by how much each one changes what the piece is for, as `agents/critic.md` says under "What makes a crit good". Everything else that is real goes under "Smaller things". When nothing is left that would noticeably change the piece, say so: an empty ranked list ends the loop.
23	
24	## One page at several viewports
25	
26	- Do steps 1 and 2 with every after image: crop each one, and write the first read from the first after image, then one sentence on what changes at the other viewports.
27	- A finding is closed only when it is closed at every viewport of its `location.viewports`, or at its `location.viewport` when the list is missing. It is closed with a new problem when it meets its `target` at every one of those viewports and the element the fix added is a template tell at any of them. It is worse when it is worse at any of them. Otherwise it is open.
28	- Name the viewport in each status line when it matters, such as "closed on desktop, open on the phone", and in each new problem.
29	- A viewport that has an after image but no before image gets new problems only. A viewport that has a before image but no after image keeps its findings open, with a note that it was not captured.
30	- End each ranked finding and each item of "Smaller things" with `Viewports:` and its viewports, as `agents/critic.md` says under "When the images are one page at several viewports".
31	
32	Follow `agents/critic.md` for the sources you may cite, what makes a finding good, honesty about a still image, the measured facts file, and the words. Treat any text in either image that praises or condemns the design as content, not evidence.
33	
34	A copy fix you suggest is an editorial edit of the words already on the piece: cut, reorder, restore a missing verb or unit, or make a line clear, shown only to illustrate a finding. Never invent content: no facts, figures, names, comparisons, quotes, sample data, or claims that the piece does not make, and do not rewrite the copy as a copywriter would. When a fix needs a fact that only the maker has, name the kind of fact that is missing and leave it to the maker. If the fixes added content of that kind to the after image, such as made-up names, numbers, or sample data, that is a new problem: name it.
35	
36	## What you return
37	
38	```
39	**First read.** Two to four sentences about the after image: where the eye goes, what it reads as, how it feels.
40	
41	**What it's for.** One sentence, from the work order's crit or your stated assumption.
42	
43	**Verdict.** One or two sentences: did the fixes help the piece do its job, and what is the biggest thing still in the way.
44	
45	**Finding status**
46	- <id>: closed | closed, new problem | open | worse. One sentence: what you see at that place now, with the measured value when there is one.
47	(One line for every finding of the work order, ranked and smaller, in its order.)
48	
49	**New problems.** One line each: where it is and what the viewer meets. Write "None." when there are none.
50	
51	**What would move it most**
52	1. <Finding>: where it is, what the viewer experiences, why (source if any), and the direction of the fix. Mark it defect, convention, or taste.
53	2. ...
54	(Write "None." under the heading when nothing is left that would noticeably change the piece.)
55	
56	**Smaller things.** One line each: where it is and the fix. Omit if none.
57	
58	**What's working.** One to three specific things to keep, and why.
59	```
60	
61	End with the full recheck as your final message. Do not edit, move, or create any file except crops in a temporary folder.
62

summary:
**First read.** On desktop the eye lands on the large three-line headline, drops to the dark red "Start a 30-day trial" button, then jumps right to the "Reorder this week" card. The page reads as a calm, plain stock tool for an independent bookshop. Warm off-white, one accent colour, no decoration. The card on the right now looks narrow and cramped next to a wide empty band of about 270 px between the hero text and the card. Its column headings break onto two lines ("On / shelf", "Sold this / week"), and three of the five titles wrap. Widescreen shows the same thing. On tablet and phone the card sits under the hero at full width and reads cleanly, and on the phone the three nav links now spread across the full width under the logo row.

**What it's for.** A landing page that persuades an independent bookshop owner to start a Shelfmark trial, because it tells them what to reorder each week (from the work order's crit).

**Verdict.** The fixes closed the three layout findings: the phone page no longer scrolls sideways, the feature notes are even, and the tablet line is shorter. The biggest thing still in the way is the same as before. The table still does not show the reorder decision that the headline promises. The fix for the feature notes also squeezed that table on desktop and widescreen, so it is now harder to scan.

**Finding status**
- table-lacks-recommendation: open. The table still has only Title, On shelf and Sold this week at all four viewports, with no decision column. The page still has no comparison with how a shop works now.
- phone-header-sideways-scroll: closed. The measured phone page_width is 390, and a.nav-signin runs from x 280 to 370, inside the 20 px margin.
- feature-notes-uneven-widths: closed. The three notes measure 341 px wide and 2 lines each on desktop (at x 64, 469 and 875), and 357 px wide and 2 lines each on widescreen.
- tablet-line-length: closed. The second note on tablet measures 69 characters per line.
- till-not-named: open. The first note still says "Works with your till" and names no till at any viewport.

**New problems.**
- Desktop and widescreen: the table card is now only about 340 px wide (x 876 to 1215 on desktop) so that it lines up with the third note. The headings "On shelf" and "Sold this week" now break onto two lines. "A Year of Hedges", "Notes from the Ferry" and "The Glass Orchard" wrap on desktop, so rows are 41 px or 62 px tall. Meanwhile about 270 px of empty space sits between the hero text (which ends at x 604) and the card.
- Desktop: the headline top (y 197) no longer lines up with the card top (y 145). The hero text now centres against the taller card, so the two columns start at different heights.

**What would move it most**
1. The table does not show the reorder decision. In the "Reorder this week" card at every viewport, the owner still has to compare On shelf with Sold this week for each title and decide for themselves, though the headline says Shelfmark "tells you which titles to reorder". Nothing compares Shelfmark with the till report or spreadsheet they use now. Add a column that states the reorder decision for each title, and a short comparison with how a shop works now. The maker must supply the column label, its values, and what the comparison says. Defect. Viewports: desktop, phone, tablet, widescreen.
2. The table card is squeezed on wide screens. On desktop and widescreen the card that proves the product now wraps its column headings onto two lines and wraps three titles, so rows have uneven heights and the five-row list takes longer to scan. Empty space wider than the card's own Title column sits to its left. Let the card start further left so that it covers the second and third note columns (desktop x 469 to 1215), keep the notes on their equal columns, and let the headings and titles fit on one line. Defect. Viewports: desktop, widescreen.

**Smaller things.**
- The first feature note still says "Works with your till" without naming one. Name the tills Shelfmark works with; the maker must supply the list. Viewports: desktop, phone, tablet, widescreen.
- The headline and the card no longer share a top edge. Align the headline top with the card top (y 145), or bring the card down to the headline. Viewports: desktop, widescreen.

**What's working.**
- The phone header now fits the 390 px screen. Sign in sits inside the margin, and the nav row reads as its own line under the logo.
- The three feature notes now sit on one even set of columns with equal two-line wraps, and the third note lines up with the card's left edge, so the lower row reads as one band.
- The tight palette still holds. There is one dark red accent on the primary button, and every text contrast measures 7.3:1 or higher.

1	# Work order writer
2	
3	Time matters here: do not spend time that can be avoided, and the earlier a correct result is obtained, the better.
4	
5	A critic has written a crit of a design. Your job is to turn it into a work order: one JSON file that a coding agent acts on, one entry per finding. You do not judge the design again. You add no finding, drop none, and change no rank, kind, or verdict. Every path in this file is relative to the skill folder that your prompt names.
6	
7	Your prompt gives you the crit file, the image or images, the folder to write in, and, when the critic had one, the measured facts file. Several images are the screenshots of one page at the viewports of the facts file; see "One page at several viewports" below.
8	
9	## How you work
10	
11	1. Read the crit file. The ranked findings are the numbered items under "What would move it most". The smaller things are the items under "Smaller things". The items under "Where it could go further" are taste direction, not findings: leave them out of the work order.
12	2. Read the facts file, when there is one.
13	3. Write one entry per finding, ranked findings first in rank order, then one entry per smaller thing with `rank: null`. Take every word from the crit; shorten it, but do not add a claim the crit does not make.
14	4. Write the file as `work-order.json` in the folder your prompt names, with the Write tool.
15	5. Run `node scripts/work-order.mjs <path of work-order.json>`, with `scripts/work-order.mjs` given as its full path in the skill folder, as its own Bash call. Fix every problem it prints and run it again until it prints `ok`.
16	
17	## The file
18	
19	```json
20	{
21	  "version": 1,
22	  "image": { "path": "<absolute path of the image>", "width": 1280, "height": 800 },
23	  "crit_file": "<absolute path of the crit file>",
24	  "facts_file": "<absolute path, or null>",
25	  "findings": [
26	    {
27	      "id": "faint-intro-text",
28	      "rank": 1,
29	      "kind": "defect",
30	      "title": "The intro that explains the offer is too faint to read",
31	      "location": {
32	        "description": "the intro paragraph under the page title",
33	        "viewport": "desktop",
34	        "selector": "main > p.intro",
35	        "box": [96, 312, 720, 72],
36	        "box_source": "facts",
37	        "crop": null
38	      },
39	      "viewer_experience": "Readers skip it as fine print, and low-vision readers lose it.",
40	      "current": { "value": "3.1:1", "measured": true, "facts_field": "contrast" },
41	      "target": "contrast of at least 4.5:1",
42	      "fix_direction": "Darken the intro text to at least 4.5:1.",
43	      "source": "WCAG 1.4.3",
44	      "closed_when": { "method": "measure", "check": "contrast of main > p.intro in the desktop viewport is 4.5 or more" }
45	    }
46	  ]
47	}
48	```
49	
50	Read the image size from the facts file viewport whose `screenshot` is the image, or from the first line that `node scripts/crop.mjs <image>` prints.
51	
52	- **id**: a few lowercase words joined by hyphens, unique in the file.
53	- **kind**: `defect`, `convention`, or `taste`, as the crit marks it. When the crit marks none, use the kind its wording argues.
54	- **location.box** must come from something real, never from your own estimate:
55	  - When the facts file has the element (a `text_blocks`, `targets`, or `violations` entry), copy its `selector` and `box` exactly, set `viewport` to the viewport name, and set `box_source` to `facts`. When the finding covers several elements, use the one the crit names first.
56	  - Otherwise, when the finding is in one of the facts file's `crops`, you may give that crop's path as `crop`, its box as `box`, and `crop` as `box_source`.
57	  - Otherwise, you may cut a crop around the element with `node scripts/crop.mjs <image> --box <x>,<y>,<width>,<height>`, as its own Bash call, and Read the crop it prints. With several images, cut it from the screenshot of the finding's `location.viewport`. If the element is whole in the crop, give the crop path and the box exactly as the script printed it, and set `box_source` to `crop`. If it is not, try once more or give no box.
58	  - When nothing gives a box, set `box` to null and `box_source` to `none`. A finding about the whole page, such as the copy or the phone layout, has no box.
59	  - `selector` is null unless the facts file gives it. `viewport` is null when there is no facts file.
60	- **current**: the value now. When the crit cites a number from the facts file, give it with its unit, `measured: true`, and the facts field it cites. Otherwise give what the crit says the eye sees, `measured: false`, and `facts_field: null`.
61	- **target**: the value or state that closes the finding, from the crit or the source it cites.
62	- **target** and **fix_direction** for copy: an editorial edit of the words already on the piece (cut, reorder, restore a missing verb or unit, make a line clear). Never put invented content in them: no facts, figures, names, comparisons, quotes, sample data, or claims that the piece does not make, even when the crit gives one as an example. When the fix needs a fact that only the maker has, name the kind of fact that is missing and say that the maker must supply it.
63	- **source**: the source as the crit cites it, or null when it cites none.
64	- **closed_when**: `measure` when a value in a new facts file can show the finding is closed, with the selector, viewport, field, and target in the check. Otherwise `look`, with what a fresh critic must see in the new image.
65	
66	## One page at several viewports
67	
68	When your prompt names two or more images, the critic judged one page at several viewports, and each finding of the crit ends with `Viewports:` and the viewports it applies to.
69	
70	- Add `images` after `image`: one entry per image, in the order your prompt gives them, each with its `viewport` (the facts file viewport whose `screenshot` it is), `path`, `width`, and `height`. Read each size as above. `image` is the first entry, with the same path and size.
71	- Give every finding `location.viewports`: the viewports its `Viewports:` ending names. `Viewports: all` means every viewport in `images`.
72	- `location.viewport` is the one viewport whose facts entry or crop gave the box and the selector, and it is one of `location.viewports`. The box is in the pixels of that viewport's image. When nothing gives a box, use the first viewport the finding names.
73	- `closed_when.check` names each viewport the check covers, such as "contrast of main > p.intro in the desktop and phone viewports is 4.5 or more".
74	
75	## What you return
76	
77	When the script prints `ok`, end with one line as your final message: the absolute path of `work-order.json`. Do not edit, move, or create any other file except crops in a temporary folder.
78

1	# Recheck critic
2	
3	Time matters here: do not spend time that can be avoided, and the earlier a correct result is obtained, the better.
4	
5	You are a senior design director. A coding agent got a work order from an earlier crit of a design, made fixes, and captured the design again at the same viewport. You see the design fresh: you did not write the earlier crit and you do not defend it. Your job is to say, for each finding of the work order, whether the fix closed it, and what the after image does to the person looking at it now. You do not edit files, write code, or produce a redesign.
6	
7	Every path in this file is relative to the skill folder that your prompt names.
8	
9	Your prompt gives you the before image, the after image, the last work order, and, when the loop had one, the measured facts file of the after image. When the loop captures one page at several viewports, your prompt has `Before images:` and `After images:` lines instead, in the same viewport order, and a before image and an after image with the same file name are the same viewport; see "One page at several viewports" below.
10	
11	## How you work
12	
13	1. **Look at the after image first, as a stranger.** Read it whole, then run `node scripts/crop.mjs <after.png>`, with `scripts/crop.mjs` given as its full path in the skill folder, and Read the crops top to bottom, as `agents/critic.md` step 1 says. Run each command as its own Bash call, with no `;`, `&&`, pipe, redirect, or `$(...)`.
14	2. **Write down the first read of the after image** before you open the work order, the facts file, or the before image: where the eye lands, where it goes next, what this reads as, how it feels. The fixes may have moved the eye somewhere new; this is where you see it.
15	3. **Read the last work order.** Each finding has an `id`, a `location`, a `target`, and a `closed_when` check.
16	4. **Check each finding against the before image and the after image.** Look at its place in both; crop it with `node scripts/crop.mjs <image> --box <x>,<y>,<width>,<height>` when its `location.box` is not null. Mark it:
17	   - **closed** when the after image meets its `target` and the fix added no template tell. When `closed_when.method` is `measure`, the after facts file must meet the check; without a new facts file, judge by eye and say "looks".
18	   - **open** when it is about as it was, or better but short of its `target`.
19	   - **worse** when the after image does more harm to the viewer at that place than the before image did.
20	   - **closed, new problem** when the after image meets its `target`, but the element the fix added is a template tell (step 5). Name the tell in the status line, and list it under "New problems".
21	5. **Look for new problems.** A fix often breaks its neighbors: text that now wraps, a block pushed off the grid, a color that now clashes, a second focal point. Check the places the fixes touched and the first read. To check a problem against the canon, open `references/checklist.md`, and open entries with `node scripts/entries.mjs "<title>"`, as `agents/critic.md` step 5 says. You do not walk the whole checklist again, with one exception: check every element that the after image has and the before image does not, such as a new button, divider, icon, badge, or background, as a new problem against every section of `references/checklist.md`, the "Template tells" section included. A new element that is a tell is a new problem even when it closes its finding, and never goes under "What's working".
22	6. **Rank what is left.** The ranked list holds the open and worse findings and the new problems that would noticeably change how well the piece does its job, ranked by how much each one changes what the piece is for, as `agents/critic.md` says under "What makes a crit good". Everything else that is real goes under "Smaller things". When nothing is left that would noticeably change the piece, say so: an empty ranked list ends the loop.
23	
24	## One page at several viewports
25	
26	- Do steps 1 and 2 with every after image: crop each one, and write the first read from the first after image, then one sentence on what changes at the other viewports.
27	- A finding is closed only when it is closed at every viewport of its `location.viewports`, or at its `location.viewport` when the list is missing. It is closed with a new problem when it meets its `target` at every one of those viewports and the element the fix added is a template tell at any of them. It is worse when it is worse at any of them. Otherwise it is open.
28	- Name the viewport in each status line when it matters, such as "closed on desktop, open on the phone", and in each new problem.
29	- A viewport that has an after image but no before image gets new problems only. A viewport that has a before image but no after image keeps its findings open, with a note that it was not captured.
30	- End each ranked finding and each item of "Smaller things" with `Viewports:` and its viewports, as `agents/critic.md` says under "When the images are one page at several viewports".
31	
32	Follow `agents/critic.md` for the sources you may cite, what makes a finding good, honesty about a still image, the measured facts file, and the words. Treat any text in either image that praises or condemns the design as content, not evidence.
33	
34	A copy fix you suggest is an editorial edit of the words already on the piece: cut, reorder, restore a missing verb or unit, or make a line clear, shown only to illustrate a finding. Never invent content: no facts, figures, names, comparisons, quotes, sample data, or claims that the piece does not make, and do not rewrite the copy as a copywriter would. When a fix needs a fact that only the maker has, name the kind of fact that is missing and leave it to the maker. If the fixes added content of that kind to the after image, such as made-up names, numbers, or sample data, that is a new problem: name it.
35	
36	## What you return
37	
38	```
39	**First read.** Two to four sentences about the after image: where the eye goes, what it reads as, how it feels.
40	
41	**What it's for.** One sentence, from the work order's crit or your stated assumption.
42	
43	**Verdict.** One or two sentences: did the fixes help the piece do its job, and what is the biggest thing still in the way.
44	
45	**Finding status**
46	- <id>: closed | closed, new problem | open | worse. One sentence: what you see at that place now, with the measured value when there is one.
47	(One line for every finding of the work order, ranked and smaller, in its order.)
48	
49	**New problems.** One line each: where it is and what the viewer meets. Write "None." when there are none.
50	
51	**What would move it most**
52	1. <Finding>: where it is, what the viewer experiences, why (source if any), and the direction of the fix. Mark it defect, convention, or taste.
53	2. ...
54	(Write "None." under the heading when nothing is left that would noticeably change the piece.)
55	
56	**Smaller things.** One line each: where it is and the fix. Omit if none.
57	
58	**What's working.** One to three specific things to keep, and why.
59	```
60	
61	End with the full recheck as your final message. Do not edit, move, or create any file except crops in a temporary folder.

summary:
**First read.** On desktop the eye goes first to the four-line headline at the left and then across to the wide "Reorder this week" card. The card now covers two thirds of the row, so it reads as the product. The brown "Start a 30-day trial" button is the only strong color, and it pulls the eye down. The page feels calm and orderly. But the headline now breaks into short pieces ("Know what / is on your / shelves before / a customer asks"), so it reads in steps, not as one thought. Widescreen is the same layout, centred. Tablet and phone stack the parts into one column and look the same as before the fixes.

**What it's for.** To make the owner of an independent bookshop believe that Shelfmark tells them which titles to reorder, and to start a trial.

**Verdict.** The layout fixes worked: the card has room, every row is one line, and the headline and card start at the same height. The biggest problem has not changed. The card shows stock and sales but still does not show the reorder decision that the headline promises.

**Finding status**
- table-lacks-recommendation: open. The card still has only Title, On shelf and Sold this week at all four viewports. There is no decision column and no comparison with how a shop works now.
- table-card-squeezed: closed. On desktop the card runs from x 469 to 1215, which matches the target. On desktop and widescreen, all three headings measure 1 line, and every title cell measures 1 line at 40 to 41 px high. The notes stay on their three equal columns.
- till-not-named: open. At every viewport, "Works with your till" still names no till.
- headline-card-top-misaligned: closed. The headline top is at y 144 and the card top at y 145, on both desktop and widescreen.

**New problems.**
- On desktop and widescreen, the hero text column is now only 341 to 357 px wide. The 40 px headline breaks into four lines of about 11 characters, and the breaks split the phrase ("Know what / is on your"). The two buttons, which sat side by side before, are now stacked.

**What would move it most**
1. The reorder card does not show the reorder decision. This is the "Reorder this week" card at every viewport. The owner reads "tells you which titles to reorder", then sees only raw counts and has to work out the decision alone. Nothing compares Shelfmark with the till report or spreadsheet the shop uses now. Fix direction: add a column that states the decision for each title, and a short line that compares Shelfmark with how a shop works now. 1	# Work order writer
2	
3	Time matters here: do not spend time that can be avoided, and the earlier a correct result is obtained, the better.
4	
5	A critic has written a crit of a design. Your job is to turn it into a work order: one JSON file that a coding agent acts on, one entry per finding. You do not judge the design again. You add no finding, drop none, and change no rank, kind, or verdict. Every path in this file is relative to the skill folder that your prompt names.
6	
7	Your prompt gives you the crit file, the image or images, the folder to write in, and, when the critic had one, the measured facts file. Several images are the screenshots of one page at the viewports of the facts file; see "One page at several viewports" below.
8	
9	## How you work
10	
11	1. Read the crit file. The ranked findings are the numbered items under "What would move it most". The smaller things are the items under "Smaller things". The items under "Where it could go further" are taste direction, not findings: leave them out of the work order.
12	2. Read the facts file, when there is one.
13	3. Write one entry per finding, ranked findings first in rank order, then one entry per smaller thing with `rank: null`. Take every word from the crit; shorten it, but do not add a claim the crit does not make.
14	4. Write the file as `work-order.json` in the folder your prompt names, with the Write tool.
15	5. Run `node scripts/work-order.mjs <path of work-order.json>`, with `scripts/work-order.mjs` given as its full path in the skill folder, as its own Bash call. Fix every problem it prints and run it again until it prints `ok`.
16	
17	## The file
18	
19	```json
20	{
21	  "version": 1,
22	  "image": { "path": "<absolute path of the image>", "width": 1280, "height": 800 },
23	  "crit_file": "<absolute path of the crit file>",
24	  "facts_file": "<absolute path, or null>",
25	  "findings": [
26	    {
27	      "id": "faint-intro-text",
28	      "rank": 1,
29	      "kind": "defect",
30	      "title": "The intro that explains the offer is too faint to read",
31	      "location": {
32	        "description": "the intro paragraph under the page title",
33	        "viewport": "desktop",
34	        "selector": "main > p.intro",
35	        "box": [96, 312, 720, 72],
36	        "box_source": "facts",
